Reference for the Rust embedded stack introduced in
[Your first embedded device](/docs/build/embedded/first-device). The firmware it describes is
[`esp32-embassy-demo`](https://github.com/arkitektio/esp32-embassy-demo).

## The crates

Embedded devices use the [Rust client](/docs/build/rust/first-app), built without the standard
library. The app-facing API is the one in the [Rust reference](/docs/build/rust/reference):
`#[action]`, typed ports, `Task`, `StateMut<T>` and the lifecycle hooks.

| Layer | Crate |
|---|---|
| The app: `App`, `#[action]`, `#[derive(State)]` | `arkitekt-spec` |
| Connecting and serving on a platform | `arkitekt-core` (`Runtime`) |
| The embassy platform: login, agent, HTTP, WebSocket, TLS | `arkitekt-embassy` (`Board`, `Embassy`, `NetHost`) |
| Bluetooth provisioning | `arkitekt-ble-provisioning` |
| The mesh (optional) | `arkitekt-mesh-embassy` |

Below those, the demo uses the Rust ecosystem's own drivers for the chip: `esp-hal` for the
peripherals, `esp-radio` for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, `embassy-net` for IP, and `esp-storage` for
flash.

## What the board provides

A desktop has an operating system. A board has to hand the runtime four things itself:

| | Why |
|---|---|
| A TCP client and DNS | Every connection to the platform. The demo uses `embassy-net`. |
| Randomness | TLS, ids and `task.random`. The demo uses the chip's hardware RNG. |
| A wall clock | Certificates are checked against the date. The demo sets it over SNTP after Wi-Fi is up. |
| Trusted root certificates | Which servers the device believes. See [TLS](#tls). |

These go into `Board`, and `Runtime::connect(board, app, options)` logs the app in and returns a
runtime whose `serve()` runs the agent. Porting to another chip means providing those four things.
The app code does not change.

## Provisioning and login

A device has no browser, so it cannot go through the approval page a desktop app opens. Instead it
is **provisioned** once:

1. From boot the device advertises `ARKITEKT-xxxx` over Bluetooth and exposes its app identifier,
   version and device id.
2. In Orkestrator, **Lok → Provision a device** reads those, issues a key for exactly that device
   and app, and sends one document: the Wi-Fi credentials, the address of the deployment and the
   key.
3. The device stores the document in its own flash partition (`arkitekt`).

On every boot it joins the Wi-Fi, sets its clock, and logs in with the stored key. The login is
ordinary [Fakts](/docs/build/fakts-protocol): the device receives a token and the addresses of
the services, opens the [agent socket](/docs/build/agent-protocol) and registers.

The device reports where it is in that sequence over Bluetooth, so Orkestrator can show it:
`registered`, or `wifi_failed`, or `login_failed:<reason>`.

**WPA2-Enterprise** (PEAP/TTLS, for example eduroam) is supported, with the identity, anonymous
identity and CA certificate taken from Orkestrator. Without a CA the RADIUS server is not verified.

**Reset.** Hold BOOT for 5 seconds while the device starts. Its configuration and login are erased
and it can be provisioned again.

## TLS [#tls]

The login (`https://`) and the agent (`wss://`) use TLS 1.3 or 1.2, and **the server's certificate
is verified**. The device trusts the root certificates compiled into the firmware. The demo ships
the Let's Encrypt roots. For a deployment behind another certificate authority, add its root in
DER form to the firmware's `certs/` directory and to its list of roots:

```sh
openssl x509 -in root.pem -outform der -out certs/my-root.der
```

Verifying a certificate chain costs a microcontroller about a second per signature. Sessions are
resumed, and the login keeps its connection open between requests, so the device checks a server's
chain once per boot and not once per request.

## Memory

Memory is the constraint that shapes the firmware:

| | Heap |
|---|---|
| Wi-Fi | about 50 KiB |
| Each TLS connection (the login's, the agent's) | 33 KiB of record buffers |
| Bluetooth | its share, until it is switched off |

This is why Bluetooth goes off 5 seconds after the device registers. On the classic ESP32, where
Bluetooth and Wi-Fi together leave very little, Bluetooth goes off *before* the login.
Orkestrator's provisioning page then reports the device as out of reach, and its Devices page
shows it registering.

## The mesh

With the `mesh` feature, an ESP32-S3 with PSRAM joins the deployment's
[mesh](/docs/run/security/mesh) and reaches services that are only available there, the same way
a desktop app does. It needs about 200 KiB of heap while on the mesh, which is why it requires
PSRAM. This variant is built but has not yet been run on a board.

```sh
cargo esp32s3 --features mesh
```

## What is not there yet [#what-is-not-there-yet]

| | Status |
|---|---|
| Workflows, calling other actions | Not supported, as in the [desktop Rust client](/docs/build/rust/reference#status) |
| Service clients such as Mikro | Not on a board. A device offers actions and state. It does not read or write images. |
| A journal that survives a reboot | Not on a board. A device that reboots mid-task leaves the task [lost](/docs/about/terminology#states). |
| EAP-TLS (client certificates) for enterprise Wi-Fi | Not supported |
| Encrypting the provisioning document over Bluetooth | Not yet |
| Over-the-air firmware updates | Not yet |
| The mesh on the classic ESP32 | Not possible without PSRAM |
| Published crates | The demo still builds against sibling checkouts of some crates |
| Other chips | Only the ESP32 and ESP32-S3 are wired up. Other embassy targets need their own `Board`. |
